The honest answer is that the tools replaced the typing, and typing was never the job. They took the slow, repetitive half of the afternoon, and I am not going to pretend I miss it. What they did not replace is deciding what should be built in the first place, and noticing, three seconds after you read it, that the answer in front of you is confidently wrong. That second one is the whole skill, and it is invisible until it is missing. On my own teams, the people who get stuck are the ones who cannot read the output. They are likely to be fine for months and then stop dead at exactly the moment the tool is wrong, which is the worst possible moment to discover that you were never reading. I say likely, and I mean likely, because I have only seen it on my own teams and that is not evidence, that is experience. And the one prediction I refuse to make is which jobs disappear. Anybody who hands you a list is selling you something, because nobody predicted the last change either, including the people who were paid to.

In the first ten minutes I am not listening for what the candidate knows. I am listening for how they talk about what they do not know, because in my experience the second thing predicts the first year far better than the first thing does. The answer that ends an interview badly is total certainty about everything. If somebody is equally sure about the framework they use daily and about the future of the whole industry, I stop believing both. What I want instead is somebody who says what they would check first, and how they would find out. And please, tell your students this: saying I do not know is not the problem. It has never once been the problem. The problem is stopping there. I am not waiting for the three words, I am waiting for the sentence that comes after them, and about half the time it never arrives.
